overview: These map labels cover the Indigenous Canary Islands, whose settlers came from North Africa. Strictly, Guanches names the people of Tenerife. Other islands developed distinct communities. The imported spans, 1500 BCE to 500 CE and 800 to 1878, are not reliable settlement or independence dates.

periods.title: Settlement in the first centuries CE
periods.summary: Radiocarbon models place Indigenous colonization in the early centuries CE; the precise sequence remains debated.

periods.title: Distinct island communities
periods.summary: Farming, herding and local environments shaped different island societies.

periods.title: Conquest and its aftermath
periods.summary: Castilian expansion ended Tenerife’s independent territories in 1496. Indigenous survivors participated in the society that followed.

items.text: A 2024 study assembled reliable radiocarbon dates to distinguish earlier Roman activity from permanent North African settlement. Its results place Indigenous colonization in the first centuries CE. The map’s 1500 BCE starting point cannot be treated as an established Guanche founding date.

Late preconquest Tenerife had nine territories. Leaders described in historical accounts as menceyes mediated disputes over pasture, watering places and herds. A ruler’s working day could involve deciding whose goats belonged at the water source, as well as negotiating alliances.

At Los Cabezazos in Tegueste, a cave used from the sixth century CE offered shelter near water and pasture. Tenerife also had stone huts: the circular or oval examples at Ifara used dry stone walls without mortar.

Obsidian, a shiny volcanic glass, supplied sharp flakes called tabonas. Craftspeople could cut with these tools without metal blades. Basalt and other stone also served everyday work, including grinding grain and processing animal products.
Goat leg bones became pointed awls, needles and spatulas for working skins, plant fibres and pottery. A herd therefore supplied materials for a household tool kit as well as milk and meat.

Leather preserved mainly in funerary caves includes decorated pieces and repairs. Those patches show that useful material was worth mending. Even an archaeological museum can contain evidence of someone deciding that an old piece still had life in it.

Archaeobotanists have identified barley, durum wheat, lentils, broad beans, peas and figs across the archipelago’s early farming evidence. These crops did not remain equally common everywhere: each island’s food history needs its own evidence.

On Gran Canaria, dried figs survived in cave granaries, while tiny fig seeds also lodged in ancient dental cavities. Teeth can preserve an unexpectedly personal trace of a meal, although tooth decay itself was no treat.

Gran Canaria’s Risco Caído mountain landscape contains cave homes, granaries and cisterns. These spaces linked shelter, stored food and water within a difficult landscape of cliffs and ravines; a cave could be useful far beyond simply keeping the rain off.

The same landscape preserves sanctuaries, rock art and Libyco-Berber inscriptions. They are material evidence of religious and written traditions. They should not be collapsed into the political history of Tenerife simply because the map uses one broad label.

In his 1510 will, Juan Azanos named two sons as heirs. One had been taken captive and converted; his father knew his earlier name, Gualçitca, but not his new one. The document makes the separation of a family painfully concrete.

A written sample is “yo, Juan Azanos, guanche”: “I, Juan Azanos, a Guanche.” It opens his will of 18 November 1510, preserved in a modern scholarly transcription. This is Spanish notarial writing; the document names interpreters who understood his language, rather than claiming that he wrote Spanish himself.

ending.text: Tenerife’s independent territories ended with the Castilian conquest in 1496, but Guanche people did not simply disappear. Records document survivors, families, land allocations and continuing place names. The imported 1878 endpoint is not the date of conquest or of an Indigenous people’s extinction.
